parakeet: This internal friction is known as cognitive dissonance. When reality directly contradicts a core belief, the brain experiences genuine physical stress. If this moves from a temporary mental itch to a chronic state, it triggers the body's HPA axis, the same system that handles fight or flight responses to physical danger. Constantly performing mental gymnastics to protect an internal map from an encroaching external reality keeps the body in a state of allostatic load. This chronic elevation of cortisol and adrenaline leads to measurable cardiovascular strain, high blood pressure, and a suppressed immune system. Your body eventually sends you the bill for the comfort of being comfortably wrong in the form of burnout and physical illness. The physical power of belief is further demonstrated by the placebo and nocebo effects. These are not all in your head. They're biological responses where the expectation of healing can trigger actual physiological recovery, while the expectation of harm, the nocebo effect, can cause a person to experience genuine side effects from a harmless substance. This intersects with your locus of control or whether you believe you're the driver of your life or a passenger. This fundamental belief dictates your levels of anxiety and depression. Believing you have no agency over your world can lead to profound psychological fragmentation and moral injury, especially when trying to maintain a double life, to satisfy a rigid social or religious group. Ultimately, the physical stress of protecting a flawed internal map leads to sociological alienation. To avoid the pain of being wrong, people often retreat into echo chambers, shrinking their social circles to avoid anyone who might challenge their views. This leads to a loss of empathy and a decreased ability to function in a pluralistic society. The result is a state of profound loneliness, which health experts note carries a mortality risk equivalent to smoking 15 cigarettes a day. When we prioritize the comfort of our beliefs over the accuracy of our evidence, we don't just lose our grip on reality, we lose our connection to each other.
